title: Worsening Shortness of Breath and Confusion
presentation: A 58-year-old male with a history of severe COPD, opioid use disorder (methadone maintenance), and recent hip arthroplasty (2 weeks prior) presents to the emergency department complaining of worsening shortness of breath, confusion, and increased productive cough for the past 48 hours. On arrival, he is tachypneic (RR 28), tachycardic (HR 110), hypoxic (SpO2 88% on room air), and appears mildly cyanotic with accessory muscle use. His temperature is 37.1 C.

stages.label: History
stages.text: He reports feeling increasingly breathless over the past few days, particularly with exertion, along with subjective confusion and increasing sputum production. He denies pleuritic chest pain, hemoptysis, or significant orthopnea. He has been taking his usual methadone maintenance dose (typically 80mg daily) and furosemide 40mg daily. He has had several hospitalizations for COPD exacerbations in the past year, including one for pneumonia 3 months ago. Social history includes heavy alcohol use and occasional marijuana smoking. He was recently discharged from the orthopedic ward after his hip replacement surgery. He states he has been using less methadone recently due to side effects but still takes it regularly. He is currently receiving supplemental oxygen via nasal cannula set to 2 liters per minute.
stages.prompt: What are your key questions regarding his history and medications?

stages.label: Exam
stages.text: On examination, the patient is alert but disoriented to place and time. Vital signs remain RR 28, HR 110, BP 130/70, SpO2 88% on RA. Lung auscultation reveals diffuse wheezes bilaterally, decreased breath sounds in the right lower lobe, and rhonchi. Bowel sounds are present. There is mild bilateral ankle edema. He has no jugular venous distension. Neurological exam is non-focal. Oxygen saturation improves to 92% on 2L nasal cannula, but he remains tachypneic and confused.
stages.prompt: Does the physical exam change your initial differential diagnosis? What is the most important test to perform next?

stages.label: Results
stages.text: Arterial Blood Gas (ABG) shows pH 7.25, pCO2 65 mmHg, HCO3 32 mEq/L, and calculated serum osmolality 290 mOsm/kg. Serum lipase is 150 IU/L. Chest X-ray demonstrates hyperinflation, flattened diaphragms, cardiomegaly, and a small left pleural effusion. EKG shows sinus tachycardia.
stages.prompt: What does the ABG suggest, and what other investigation would help differentiate between the leading diagnoses?

diagnosis: Acute-on-chronic hypercapnic respiratory failure from obesity hypoventilation syndrome with undiagnosed obstructive sleep apnoea, worsened by opioid use and over-oxygenation in the emergency department
key_clues: Chronic hypercapnia indicated by high baseline pCO2 (likely >50 mmHg) and compensatory metabolic alkalosis (HCO3>28)
Increased pCO2 and acidosis during acute decompensation (pH < 7.35)
High serum osmolality (>295 mOsm/kg) suggests hypertonicity, often due to elevated CO2 or hyperglycemia
Physical exam findings suggestive of volume overload (ankle edema, possible pleural effusion)
History of opioid use disorder and recent hospitalization increases risk for opioid-induced respiratory depression
Over-oxygenation worsens respiratory distress and hypercapnia
COPD exacerbation is common, but the chronicity of hypercapnia points towards OHS/OSA is the primary driver of the hypercapnia
Absence of significant neutrophilia or leukocytosis doesn't rule out bacterial pneumonia, but clinical picture is less compelling than OHS/OSA contribution

distractors.name: COPD exacerbation with respiratory acidosis
distractors.why_not: While COPD is present, the chronic hypercapnia suggests OHS/OSA is the primary driver of the hypercapnia.

distractors.name: Pulmonary embolism
distractors.why_not: No classic PE symptoms like pleuritic chest pain or hemoptysis; CXR findings don't suggest PE.

distractors.name: Heart failure exacerbation
distractors.why_not: Ankle edema and cardiomegaly are present, but JVD is absent, and the prominent hypercapnia is better explained by OHS/OSA.

distractors.name: Sepsis
distractors.why_not: Temperature is normal, no clear source of infection identified yet, although pneumonia cannot be ruled out entirely.

distractors.name: Drug overdose
distractors.why_not: Methadone level would be needed, but history of OHS/OSA makes this less likely as the sole cause, especially with the gradual onset and known history.

rubric.description: Final diagnosis is Acute-on-chronic hypercapnic respiratory failure from obesity hypoventilation syndrome with undiagnosed obstructive sleep apnoea

management_summary: The patient presents with acute-on-chronic hypercapnic respiratory failure likely driven by Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome (OHS) exacerbated by opioid use and potentially an infectious trigger (pneumonia). Initial management involves non-invasive ventilation (NIV) to improve ventilation and reduce work of breathing, careful administration of supplemental oxygen targeting SpO2 88-90%, initiation of loop diuretics for volume overload, and reduction of opioid dosage. Given the moderate severity of symptoms (confusion, tachypnea), a 100-150 mL bolus of 3% hypertonic saline is administered to raise the pH, followed by reassessment and potentially further boluses if needed. The goal is to correct the pH by 4-6 mEq/L in the first 6 hours and limit overall correction to 8 mEq/L in 24 hours. Subsequently, fluid restriction and treatment of the underlying trigger (likely infection) are initiated. Hospital admission is required for monitoring and management. Imaging (CT chest) and tissue sampling are planned for the hilar mass.
teaching_points: Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome (OHS) is characterized by chronic daytime hypercapnia (PaCO2 > 45 mmHg) without overt obesity (BMI < 30) or neuromuscular disease, primarily due to inadequate ventilation.
Undiagnosed Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA) frequently coexists with OHS and contributes significantly to the chronic hypercapnia.
Acute exacerbations of OHS/OSA often occur due to triggers like infections (pneumonia), opioids, alcohol, or metabolic stress.
Patients with OHS/OSA have impaired ability to respond to hypoxia, making them susceptible to over-oxygenation which worsens hypercapnia.
The management focuses on improving ventilation (NIV), addressing volume status, reducing opioid load, treating the trigger, and carefully managing oxygenation.
For moderate to severe symptoms of hypercapnic respiratory failure, hypertonic saline is used cautiously to raise pH, but the correction rate must be limited to prevent complications.
